items.stem: Which sample is most likely to represent all the students in a school?
items.answer: a random sample from every year group
items.markingKey: a random sample from every year group. Random selection across the population reduces bias.

items.stem: "Shoe size is continuous because feet can be any length." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Shoe sizes only take set values (e.g. 38, 38.5, 39), so shoe size is discrete.
items.markingKey: Shoe sizes only take set values (e.g. 38, 38.5, 39), so shoe size is discrete. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as qualitative, quantitative discrete or quantitative continuous: (a) the temperature at noon in a city, (b) the number of cars passing a school in an hour, (c) the number of goals scored in a match.
items.answer: (a) quantitative, continuous; (b) quantitative, discrete; (c) quantitative, discrete
items.markingKey: A1 for each correct classification (continuous = measured, discrete = counted / set values).

items.stem: A school in Singapore has 60 students in Grade 12, 180 in Grade 11 and 90 in Grade 7. A sample of 30 students is chosen so that each grade is represented in proportion. How many students should be chosen from each grade?
items.answer: Grade 12: 5, Grade 11: 16, Grade 7: 8
items.markingKey: Fraction of the total for each grade × 30 (M1); 5.455, 16.36, 8.182 rounded (A1); total 29 checked (A1).

items.stem: An international school in Singapore has 900 students. The student council wants to investigate time spent reading. (a) Write one suitable, unbiased survey question with non-overlapping response boxes. (b) Describe how to choose a random sample of 50 students. (c) Explain one possible source of bias and how to reduce it. (d) State whether the data collected will be discrete, continuous or qualitative.
items.answer: (a) e.g. a clear question with a time period and non-overlapping options (b) number the students 1–900 and use a random number generator to pick 50 different numbers (c) e.g. only surveying one grade – stratify by grade (d) depends on the question: time/amount is continuous (often recorded in groups), travel mode is qualitative
items.markingKey: Question unbiased with complete, non-overlapping options (A1 C1); random sampling method described (M1 A1); bias identified and addressed (R1); data type (A1).

items.stem: Which of these is an example of discrete data?
items.answer: the number of siblings
items.markingKey: B. The number of siblings is discrete.

items.stem: A sports shop in Seoul asks customers "Do you agree that exercise is important?" Explain why this is a poor survey question.
items.answer: It is a leading question that encourages "yes"; it gives no measurable information; the sample (shop customers) is already interested in sport.
items.markingKey: It is a leading question that encourages "yes"; it gives no measurable information; the sample (shop customers) is already interested in sport. (R1 for each valid, explained problem; criterion C: clear explanation).

items.stem: Distinguish between a population and a sample.
items.answer: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is a smaller part of it used to draw conclusions about the whole.
items.markingKey: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is a smaller part of it used to draw conclusions about the whole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Felix writes: "Asking your friends is a good random sample of your school." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Friends share similar interests and year group, so the sample is biased; a random method is needed.
items.markingKey: Friends share similar interests and year group, so the sample is biased; a random method is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as qualitative, quantitative discrete or quantitative continuous: (a) the temperature at noon in a city, (b) the mass of a newborn baby, (c) favourite type of music.
items.answer: (a) quantitative, continuous; (b) quantitative, continuous; (c) qualitative
items.markingKey: A1 for each correct classification (continuous = measured, discrete = counted / set values).

items.stem: "An online poll is the best way to find out what all the people in a city think." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is useful but biased; a random sample with a well-designed questionnaire is more representative.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is cheap and fast and can reach many people; responses are easy to analyse. Arguments against: only people with internet access and interest respond (self-selection bias); some people may vote many times. Supported judgement: It is useful but biased; a random sample with a well-designed questionnaire is more representative. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "key"?
options: The explanation of how to read a diagram, e.g. 3 | 7 means 37
A relationship between two variables: positive (both increase), negative (one increases as the other decreases) or none
A graph of plotted points showing the relationship between two numerical variables
A part of a population chosen to represent the whole population
items.answer: The explanation of how to read a diagram, e.g. 3 | 7 means 37
items.markingKey: A. "key" is the explanation of how to read a diagram, e.g. 3 | 7 means 37.

items.stem: Noah writes: "A pie chart sector of 120° always represents 120 people." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The angle shows a fraction (120/360 = 1/3) of the total; the number depends on the total frequency.
items.markingKey: The angle shows a fraction (120/360 = 1/3) of the total; the number depends on the total frequency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the angles in a pie chart must add up to 360°.
items.answer: The whole circle represents the total frequency, and a full turn is 360°.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The whole circle represents the total frequency, and a full turn is 360°. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: 72 students were asked how they travel to school: walk 12, bike 17, bus 18, car 25. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: walk 60°, bike 85°, bus 90°, car 125°
items.markingKey: Each student = 360 ÷ 72 = 5° (M1); all angles correct and total 360° (A1 A1).

items.stem: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows marks in a quiz for 15 students (key: 3 | 4 = 34): 2 | 1 1; 3 | 1 5 5 7; 4 | 0; 5 | 1 6 6; 6 | 1 1; 7 | 2 8 8. Find the median, the range and the mode.
items.answer: median 51, range 57, mode: 21, 35, 56, 61, 78
items.markingKey: Median is the 8th value (M1) = 51 (A1); range 78 − 21 = 57 (A1); mode: 21, 35, 56, 61, 78 (A1).

items.stem: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the reaction times (hundredths of a second) of 12 students before (left) and after (right) a training game (key: 3 | 4 means 34 on either side): 8 6 5 4 | 3 | 1; 9 7 | 4 | 2 2 2 5 6 9; 5 | 5 | 3 6; 6 3 | 6 | 7; 9 2 1 | 7 | 5 9. (a) Find the median and range for each group. (b) Compare the two distributions. (c) Explain why a back-to-back diagram is useful here.
items.answer: (a) before: median 52, range 45; after: median 47.5, range 48 (b) times were lower (better) after; before is more consistent (c) both groups share stems, so shape and values can be compared directly
items.markingKey: Medians and ranges (A1 A1 A1 A1); comparison of average and spread in context (R1 R1); communication (C1).

items.stem: A pie chart represents 60 people. How many people does a sector of 30° represent?
Briefly explain why a pie chart is not suitable for showing changes over time.
items.answer: A pie chart compares parts of one whole at one time; changes over time are better shown by a line graph or bar chart.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A pie chart compares parts of one whole at one time; changes over time are better shown by a line graph or bar chart. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Chloé wants to show the monthly rainfall in Kuala Lumpur over a year. Explain why a pie chart is not a good choice and suggest a better display.
items.answer: Rainfall each month is not part of a meaningful whole and the pattern over time is lost; use a bar chart or line graph with months in order.
items.markingKey: Reason pie chart unsuitable (R1); suitable alternative with reason (R1).

items.stem: "A pie chart sector of 120° always represents 120 people." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The angle shows a fraction (120/360 = 1/3) of the total; the number depends on the total frequency.
items.markingKey: The angle shows a fraction (120/360 = 1/3) of the total; the number depends on the total frequency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 24 students were asked how they travel to school: bike 3, scooter 11, walk 4, car 6. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: bike 45°, scooter 165°, walk 60°, car 90°
items.markingKey: Each student = 360 ÷ 24 = 15° (M1); all angles correct and total 360° (A1 A1).

items.stem: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows heart rates (beats per minute) after exercise for 11 students (key: 3 | 4 = 34): 2 | 1 8; 3 | 4 6; 4 | 2 4; 5 | 7; 6 | 3 9; 7 | 2 5. Find the median, the range and the mode.
items.answer: median 44, range 54, mode: none
items.markingKey: Median is the 6th value (M1) = 44 (A1); range 75 − 21 = 54 (A1); mode: none (A1).

items.stem: "The bars of a bar chart for discrete data must touch." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bars for categories or discrete values have gaps; touching bars are used for continuous data in histograms.
items.markingKey: Bars for categories or discrete values have gaps; touching bars are used for continuous data in histograms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the reaction times (hundredths of a second) of 12 students before (left) and after (right) a training game (key: 3 | 4 means 34 on either side): 9 9 | 3 | 2 8; 8 5 0 | 4 | 4 9; 9 9 0 | 5 | 2 4 7 9; 9 4 2 1 | 6 | 0 9;  | 7 | 5 8. (a) Find the median and range for each group. (b) Compare the two distributions. (c) Explain why a back-to-back diagram is useful here.
items.answer: (a) before: median 54.5, range 30; after: median 55.5, range 46 (b) times were higher after; before is more consistent (c) both groups share stems, so shape and values can be compared directly
items.markingKey: Medians and ranges (A1 A1 A1 A1); comparison of average and spread in context (R1 R1); communication (C1).

items.stem: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the reaction times (hundredths of a second) of 12 students before (left) and after (right) a training game (key: 3 | 4 means 34 on either side): 5 4 | 3 | 1; 9 9 6 3 1 | 4 | 7 8 9;  | 5 | 6 9 9; 9 7 3 2 | 6 | 7 9 9; 3 | 7 | 4 5. (a) Find the median and range for each group. (b) Compare the two distributions. (c) Explain why a back-to-back diagram is useful here.
items.answer: (a) before: median 49, range 39; after: median 59, range 44 (b) times were higher after; before is more consistent (c) both groups share stems, so shape and values can be compared directly
items.markingKey: Medians and ranges (A1 A1 A1 A1); comparison of average and spread in context (R1 R1); communication (C1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mean"?
options: Numerical data that can only take particular (usually whole-number) values, such as the number of siblings
The sum of the values divided by the number of values
A graph of plotted points showing the relationship between two numerical variables
A display that splits each value into a stem (leading digits) and a leaf (last digit), keeping the original data
items.answer: The sum of the values divided by the number of values
items.markingKey: B. "mean" is the sum of the values divided by the number of values.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "To find the mean from a frequency table, add the frequencies and divide by the number of rows." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency).
items.markingKey: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the median can be a better average than the mean for house prices.
items.answer: A few very expensive houses raise the mean a lot, while the median is the middle price and is not pulled by extreme values. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A few very expensive houses raise the mean a lot, while the median is the middle price and is not pulled by extreme values. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The minutes late of a train service were: 3, 10, 2, 27, 3, 20, 3. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
items.answer: mean 9.71, median 3, mode 3, range 25
items.markingKey: Σ = 68, ÷ 7 (M1) → mean 9.71 (A1); ordered list for median 3 (A1); mode and range (A1).

items.stem: Isabel has test scores 40, 20, 39, 6 and one more test to take. What score is needed in the last test for a mean of 29 over all 5 tests?
The table shows the number of times students visited the library last week for a group of students. Value: 2, 3, 4, 5; frequency: 8, 10, 2, 4. Find the mean (to 2 d.p.), the median and the mode.
items.answer: mean 3.08, median 3, mode 3
items.markingKey: Σfx = 74 (M1), Σf = 24 (A1); mean 3.08 (A1); median position 12.5 → 3 (A1); mode 3 (A1).

items.stem: Investigate: the mean of the numbers 1, 2, 3, …, n for n = 3, 4, 5, 6. (a) Find each mean. (b) Describe the pattern and write a formula for the mean of 1 to n. (c) Use it to find the mean of 1 to 30. (d) What happens to the mean if every number is increased by 3?
items.answer: (a) 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 (b) the mean increases by 0.5 each time: (n + 1)/2 (c) 15.5 (d) the mean also increases by 3
items.markingKey: (a) 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 (b) the mean increases by 0.5 each time: (n + 1)/2 (c) 15.5 (d) the mean also increases by 3. Averages and range calculated (M1 A1 A1); pattern/comparison in context (B/D: R1 R1); conclusion communicated (C1).

items.stem: Leila and Diego are basketball players. Points scored in their last 8 games: Leila: 23, 30, 18, 18, 15, 23, 13, 29; Diego: 6, 32, 27, 27, 8, 11, 24, 13. (a) Find the mean, median and range for each player. (b) Which player would you choose for an important match? Justify your answer using both an average and the range.
items.answer: (a) Leila: mean 21.13, median 20.5, range 17; Diego: mean 18.5, median 18.5, range 26 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics
items.markingKey: (a) Leila: mean 21.13, median 20.5, range 17; Diego: mean 18.5, median 18.5, range 26 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics. Averages and range calculated (M1 A1 A1); pattern/comparison in context (B/D: R1 R1); conclusion communicated (C1).

items.stem: What is the median of 27, 1, 9, 6, 7?
items.markingKey: C. Order the data: 1, 6, 7, 9, 27; the middle value is 7.

items.stem: The mean of four numbers is 8. What is their total?
items.markingKey: D. Total = mean × number of values.

items.stem: The annual salaries at a small company in Singapore are (Singapore dollars): 29 000, 32 000, 42 000, 45 000, 45 000, 45 000, 260 000. The manager says the "average salary" is S$71 143. Explain why this may mislead job applicants and which average is better.
items.answer: The mean S$71 143 is pulled up by one very high salary; the median S$45 000 better represents a typical worker.
items.markingKey: Mean and median calculated (A1 A1); effect of the extreme value explained (R1).

items.stem: A student claims: "To find the mean from a frequency table, add the frequencies and divide by the number of rows." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency).
items.markingKey: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the mode is the only average that can be used for qualitative data.
items.answer: Categories such as colours cannot be added or ordered, so a mean or median cannot be calculated; you can only find the most common one.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Categories such as colours cannot be added or ordered, so a mean or median cannot be calculated; you can only find the most common one. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Nia has test scores 14, 26, 13, 23, 19 and one more test to take. What score is needed in the last test for a mean of 19 over all 6 tests?

The table shows the number of times students visited the library last week for a group of students. Value: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; frequency: 6, 5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 3. Find the mean (to 2 d.p.), the median and the mode.
items.answer: mean 2.51, median 2, mode 2
items.markingKey: Σfx = 98 (M1), Σf = 39 (A1); mean 2.51 (A1); median position 20 → 2 (A1); mode 2 (A1).

items.stem: The daily maximum temperatures (°C) were: 6, 13, 29, 2, 20, 8, 10, 6. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
items.answer: mean 11.75, median 9, mode 6, range 27
items.markingKey: Σ = 94, ÷ 8 (M1) → mean 11.75 (A1); ordered list for median 9 (A1); mode and range (A1).

items.stem: The points scored by a netball shooter in recent matches were: 11, 8, 4, 6, 2, 20, 10, 8, 16. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
items.answer: mean 9.44, median 8, mode 8, range 18
items.markingKey: Σ = 85, ÷ 9 (M1) → mean 9.44 (A1); ordered list for median 8 (A1); mode and range (A1).

items.stem: Amara and Priya are basketball players. Points scored in their last 8 games: Amara: 11, 30, 18, 17, 15, 19, 30, 17; Priya: 26, 23, 29, 21, 28, 28, 32, 27. (a) Find the mean, median and range for each player. (b) Which player would you choose for an important match? Justify your answer using both an average and the range.
items.answer: (a) Amara: mean 19.63, median 17.5, range 19; Priya: mean 26.75, median 27.5, range 11 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics
items.markingKey: (a) Amara: mean 19.63, median 17.5, range 19; Priya: mean 26.75, median 27.5, range 11 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics. Averages and range calculated (M1 A1 A1); pattern/comparison in context (B/D: R1 R1); conclusion communicated (C1).

items.stem: Isabel and Yusuf are basketball players. Points scored in their last 8 games: Isabel: 24, 13, 18, 28, 21, 24, 19, 19; Yusuf: 15, 13, 21, 25, 20, 30, 19, 23. (a) Find the mean, median and range for each player. (b) Which player would you choose for an important match? Justify your answer using both an average and the range.
items.answer: (a) Isabel: mean 20.75, median 20, range 15; Yusuf: mean 20.75, median 20.5, range 17 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics
items.markingKey: (a) Isabel: mean 20.75, median 20, range 15; Yusuf: mean 20.75, median 20.5, range 17 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics. Averages and range calculated (M1 A1 A1); pattern/comparison in context (B/D: R1 R1); conclusion communicated (C1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "scatter diagram"?
options: A graph of plotted points showing the relationship between two numerical variables
The value that occurs most often
A display that splits each value into a stem (leading digits) and a leaf (last digit), keeping the original data
A chart of separated bars whose heights show the frequencies of categories or discrete values
items.answer: A graph of plotted points showing the relationship between two numerical variables
items.markingKey: A. "scatter diagram" is a graph of plotted points showing the relationship between two numerical variables.

items.stem: Explain what a strong correlation looks like on a scatter diagram.
items.answer: The points lie close to a straight line; the closer they are, the stronger the correlation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The points lie close to a straight line; the closer they are, the stronger the correlation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In summer, both ice-cream sales and sunburn cases increase. Nia concludes that one causes the other. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
items.answer: Both are caused by hot, sunny weather (a third variable); ice cream does not cause sunburn.
items.markingKey: Both are caused by hot, sunny weather (a third variable); ice cream does not cause sunburn. (R1: correlation ≠ causation; R1: plausible third variable named).

items.stem: "Negative correlation means the values are negative." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease; the values can be positive.
items.markingKey: It means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease; the values can be positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data for hours of practice (x) and score (y): (1, 51), (7, 23), (9, 53), (17, 49), (21, 52), (23, 47), (24, 39), (28, 60). Describe the correlation shown on a scatter diagram of these data and interpret it in context.
items.answer: little or no correlation
items.markingKey: Little or no correlation (A1); interpretation: no clear relationship (R1).

items.stem: A café in Oslo records the maximum daily temperature (°C, x) and the number of cold drinks sold (y): (10, 36), (13, 40), (16, 101), (20, 62), (23, 78), (26, 68), (33, 95), (34, 97). (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Identify the outlier and suggest a reason for it. (c) Ignoring the outlier, the line of best fit has gradient about 3 and passes through (22.71, 68). Estimate sales on a day with a maximum of 17 °C. (d) Explain why predicting sales on a 45 °C day is unreliable.
items.answer: (a) positive correlation (b) (16, 101) – e.g. a holiday, a power cut or a special event (c) about 50.9 drinks (d) 45 °C is outside the data range (extrapolation)
items.markingKey: Correlation described in context (A1); outlier identified with a plausible reason (A1 R1); estimate from the line (M1 A1); extrapolation explained (R1).

items.stem: What type of correlation would you expect between the number of hours of sunshine and the number of umbrellas sold?
items.answer: negative
items.markingKey: B. The number of hours of sunshine and the number of umbrellas sold: negative correlation expected.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Negative correlation means the values are negative." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease; the values can be positive.
items.markingKey: It means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease; the values can be positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel prizes. Zara concludes that one causes the other. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
items.answer: Wealthier countries can afford both more chocolate and more research funding; wealth is a confounding variable.
items.markingKey: Wealthier countries can afford both more chocolate and more research funding; wealth is a confounding variable. (R1: correlation ≠ causation; R1: plausible third variable named).

items.stem: Students who own more books get higher grades. Omar concludes that one causes the other. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
items.answer: Other factors (family support, interest in reading) may explain both; owning books does not automatically cause high grades.
items.markingKey: Other factors (family support, interest in reading) may explain both; owning books does not automatically cause high grades. (R1: correlation ≠ causation; R1: plausible third variable named).

items.stem: Data for revision hours (x) and test score (y): (2, 8), (4, 13), (6, 18), (7, 21), (10, 27), (11, 26), (16, 37). A line of best fit through the mean point has gradient 2. (a) Find the mean point. (b) Use the line to estimate the score for 7 hours of revision.
items.markingKey: Mean point (A1 A1); y − 21.43 = 2(x − 8) (M1); estimate 19.4 (A1).

items.stem: Data for hours of practice (x) and score (y): (9, 31), (12, 32), (18, 45), (20, 52), (21, 48), (24, 56), (25, 60), (29, 68). Describe the correlation shown on a scatter diagram of these data and interpret it in context.
items.answer: positive correlation
items.markingKey: Positive correlation (A1); interpretation: higher hours of practice tends to go with higher score (R1).

items.stem: Data for revision hours (x) and test score (y): (3, 26), (4, 31), (7, 44), (8, 48), (14, 71), (15, 75), (18, 84). A line of best fit through the mean point has gradient 4. (a) Find the mean point. (b) Use the line to estimate the score for 12 hours of revision.
items.markingKey: Mean point (A1 A1); y − 54.14 = 4(x − 9.857) (M1); estimate 62.7 (A1).

items.stem: A café in Melbourne records the maximum daily temperature (°C, x) and the number of cold drinks sold (y): (11, 31), (13, 32), (21, 69), (22, 65), (23, 73), (26, 71), (30, 138), (31, 94). (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Identify the outlier and suggest a reason for it. (c) Ignoring the outlier, the line of best fit has gradient about 3 and passes through (21, 62.14). Estimate sales on a day with a maximum of 25 °C. (d) Explain why predicting sales on a 45 °C day is unreliable.
items.answer: (a) positive correlation (b) (30, 138) – e.g. a holiday, a power cut or a special event (c) about 74.1 drinks (d) 45 °C is outside the data range (extrapolation)
items.markingKey: Correlation described in context (A1); outlier identified with a plausible reason (A1 R1); estimate from the line (M1 A1); extrapolation explained (R1).

items.stem: A café in Dubai records the maximum daily temperature (°C, x) and the number of cold drinks sold (y): (12, 29), (14, 32), (21, 69), (25, 35), (28, 77), (30, 88), (32, 94), (33, 91). Estimate sales on a day with a maximum of 16 °C. (d) Explain why predicting sales on a 45 °C day is unreliable.
items.answer: (a) positive correlation (b) (25, 35) – e.g. a holiday, a power cut or a special event (c) about 43.7 drinks (d) 45 °C is outside the data range (extrapolation)
items.markingKey: Correlation described in context (A1); outlier identified with a plausible reason (A1 R1); estimate from the line (M1 A1); extrapolation explained (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The value that occurs most often"?
items.answer: mode
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of mode.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A chart of separated bars whose heights show the frequencies of categories or discrete values"?
items.answer: bar chart
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of bar chart.

items.stem: Which pair of variables probably has no correlation?
options: hours of revision and test score
items.answer: shoe size and test score
items.markingKey: B. There is no reason for one to affect the other.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a larger random sample usually gives more reliable results.
items.answer: Random variation averages out over more data, so the sample statistics are closer to the population values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random variation averages out over more data, so the sample statistics are closer to the population values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The annual salaries at a small company in Melbourne are (Australian dollars): 35 000, 35 000, 36 000, 38 000, 43 000, 45 000, 397 000. The manager says the "average salary" is A$89 857. Explain why this may mislead job applicants and which average is better.
items.answer: The mean A$89 857 is pulled up by one very high salary; the median A$38 000 better represents a typical worker.
items.markingKey: Mean and median calculated (A1 A1); effect of the extreme value explained (R1).

items.stem: Two pie charts show favourite sports in two schools of 264 and 64 students. In both, football has a 90° sector. Mei says the same number of students in each school chose football. Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: 90° is a quarter in both, but a quarter of 264 is 66 and a quarter of 64 is 16.
items.markingKey: Angles show proportions, not numbers (R1); calculation (A1).

items.stem: Explain why correlation does not prove that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: Both variables may depend on a third factor (e.g. ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather), or the link may be coincidence.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both variables may depend on a third factor (e.g. ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather), or the link may be coincidence. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why response boxes in a questionnaire should not overlap.
items.answer: If boxes overlap (e.g. 0–2 and 2–4), some answers fit two boxes and the data become ambiguous.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If boxes overlap (e.g. 0–2 and 2–4), some answers fit two boxes and the data become ambiguous. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "To find the mean from a frequency table, add the frequencies and divide by the number of rows." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency).
items.markingKey: Divide Σ(value × frequency) by Σ(frequency). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 45 students were asked how they travel to school: walk 11, bike 3, scooter 14, car 17. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: walk 88°, bike 24°, scooter 112°, car 136°

items.stem: A school in Melbourne has 60 students in Grade 12, 90 in Grade 10 and 160 in Grade 8. A sample of 40 students is chosen so that each grade is represented in proportion. How many students should be chosen from each grade?
items.answer: Grade 12: 8, Grade 10: 12, Grade 8: 21

items.stem: The table shows the number of pets for a group of students. Value: 1, 2, 3, 4; frequency: 3, 9, 12, 5. Find the mean (to 2 d.p.), the median and the mode.
items.answer: mean 2.66, median 3, mode 3

items.stem: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows heart rates (beats per minute) after exercise for 13 students (key: 3 | 4 = 34): 2 | 1; 3 | 1 3 4; 4 | 1 4 4 5 6; 5 | ; 6 | 0 2 7 9. Find the median, the range and the mode.

items.stem: "A line of best fit must pass through the origin." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It passes through the middle of the points (often through the mean point), not necessarily through (0, 0).
items.markingKey: It passes through the middle of the points (often through the mean point), not necessarily through (0, 0). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Shoe size is continuous because feet can be any length." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Shoe sizes only take set values (e.g. 38, 38.5, 39), so shoe size is discrete.
items.markingKey: Shoe sizes only take set values (e.g. 38, 38.5, 39), so shoe size is discrete. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Arjun and Mei are basketball players. Points scored in their last 8 games: Arjun: 26, 11, 11, 13, 10, 18, 13, 12; Mei: 12, 31, 19, 31, 11, 31, 26, 11. (a) Find the mean, median and range for each player. (b) Which player would you choose for an important match? Justify your answer using both an average and the range.
items.answer: (a) Arjun: mean 14.25, median 12.5, range 16; Mei: mean 21.5, median 22.5, range 20 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics
items.markingKey: (a) Arjun: mean 14.25, median 12.5, range 16; Mei: mean 21.5, median 22.5, range 20 (b) choose the player with the higher average unless the other is much more consistent (smaller range) – any reasoned choice using both statistics. Averages and range calculated (M1 A1 A1); pattern/comparison in context (B/D: R1 R1); conclusion communicated (C1).

items.stem: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the reaction times (hundredths of a second) of 12 students before (left) and after (right) a training game (key: 3 | 4 means 34 on either side): 7 2 0 | 3 | 0 1 9; 9 1 0 | 4 | 5; 6 5 3 | 5 | 1 3; 4 4 0 | 6 | 0 4;  | 7 | 0 3 5 8. items.answer: (a) before: median 51, range 34; after: median 56.5, range 48 (b) times were higher after; before is more consistent (c) both groups share stems, so shape and values can be compared directly

items.stem: A café in Singapore records the maximum daily temperature (°C, x) and the number of cold drinks sold (y): (10, 82), (16, 39), (19, 49), (23, 65), (24, 75), (25, 85), (27, 77), (28, 86). (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Identify the outlier and suggest a reason for it. (c) Ignoring the outlier, the line of best fit has gradient about 3 and passes through (23.14, 68). Estimate sales on a day with a maximum of 22 °C. (d) Explain why predicting sales on a 45 °C day is unreliable.
items.answer: (a) positive correlation (b) (10, 82) – e.g. a holiday, a power cut or a special event (c) about 64.6 drinks (d) 45 °C is outside the data range (extrapolation)
items.markingKey: Correlation described in context (A1); outlier identified with a plausible reason (A1 R1); estimate from the line (M1 A1); extrapolation explained (R1).

items.stem: An international school in Nairobi has 1200 students. The student council wants to investigate sleep. (a) Write one suitable, unbiased survey question with non-overlapping response boxes. (b) Describe how to choose a random sample of 40 students. (c) Explain one possible source of bias and how to reduce it. (d) State whether the data collected will be discrete, continuous or qualitative.
items.answer: (a) e.g. a clear question with a time period and non-overlapping options (b) number the students 1–1200 and use a random number generator to pick 40 different numbers (c) e.g. only surveying one grade – stratify by grade (d) depends on the question: time/amount is continuous (often recorded in groups), travel mode is qualitative
items.markingKey: Question unbiased with complete, non-overlapping options (A1 C1); random sampling method described (M1 A1); bias identified and addressed (R1); data type (A1).

items.stem: Define the term "median".
items.answer: The middle value when the data are in order (or the mean of the two middle values)

items.answer: a stem-and-leaf diagram

items.stem: Define the term "correlation".
items.answer: A relationship between two variables: positive (both increase), negative (one increases as the other decreases) or none

items.stem: Distinguish between qualitative data and quantitative data.
items.answer: Qualitative data are categories or descriptions (e.g. favourite fruit); quantitative data are numbers from counting or measuring.
items.markingKey: Qualitative data are categories or descriptions (e.g. favourite fruit); quantitative data are numbers from counting or measuring. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how to find the mean from a frequency table.
items.answer: Multiply each value by its frequency, add these products to get the total, and divide by the total frequency.

items.stem: A sports shop in Mexico City asks customers "Do you agree that exercise is important?" Explain why this is a poor survey question.
items.answer: It is a leading question that encourages "yes"; it gives no measurable information; the sample (shop customers) is already interested in sport.
items.markingKey: It is a leading question that encourages "yes"; it gives no measurable information; the sample (shop customers) is already interested in sport. (R1 for each valid, explained problem; criterion C: clear explanation).

items.stem: A student claims: "The bars of a bar chart for discrete data must touch." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Bars for categories or discrete values have gaps; touching bars are used for continuous data in histograms.

items.stem: "An online poll is the best way to find out what all the people in a city think." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is useful but biased; a random sample with a well-designed questionnaire is more representative.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is cheap and fast and can reach many people; responses are easy to analyse. Arguments against: only people with internet access and interest respond (self-selection bias); some people may vote many times. Supported judgement: It is useful but biased; a random sample with a well-designed questionnaire is more representative. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
